issues.description: `raise PerformanceWarning(msg)` raises a Warning subclass as an exception; the test asserts via pytest.raises which works, but semantically a warning is being weaponized as an error without any path to merely warn.
issues.detail: Precondition for this branch: the configured chunk-size is incompatible with shard alignment. The author has chosen to abort with an exception named `PerformanceWarning`. Either it is a warning (in which case `warnings.warn` is the correct mechanism, and execution continues) or it is a fatal precondition violation (in which case the type should be `ValueError`, not a class whose name asserts it is a non-fatal performance hint). The current code conflates the two and forces every caller to either catch a thing called a Warning or have their program terminated. Decide which it is and use the right primitive.

issues.description: Dead `break` statement after `raise` — unreachable code, betraying that the author did not reason about the control flow.
issues.detail: Inside the per-axis loop, the body reads `raise PerformanceWarning(msg)` followed by `break`. A raise unwinds the stack; the break cannot execute. Either the author intended to warn-and-continue (in which case the raise is wrong) or intended to abort (in which case the break is wrong). Either way, the presence of both is proof the author did not state the postcondition of the loop and reason about which exit edges are live. UNREASONED.

issues.description: `safe_chunk_size` formula uses `np.prod(zarr_write_chunks)` across all axes for a per-axis diagnostic, which is dimensionally incoherent.
issues.detail: The loop iterates over axes and complains that axis `ax` is misaligned with `zw` (a scalar shard extent on that axis). The remediation message then computes `safe_chunk_size = np.prod(zarr_write_chunks) * max(1, z.dtype.itemsize)` — the product over every axis. For a 3D array with shard shape (s0,s1,s2), the suggested config value is s0*s1*s2*itemsize bytes, which is the size of one whole shard, not the per-axis quantity the loop is reasoning about. Either the postcondition is `array.chunk-size >= one full shard in bytes` (in which case the loop should not be per-axis at all, and only one message should be emitted) or it is per-axis, in which case the formula is wrong. State the postcondition, then write the formula.

issues.description: Predicate `not nominal_dask_chunk_size % zw == 0` relies on Python operator precedence rather than parentheses; reads as a smuggled goto for the reviewer's eye.
issues.detail: `not X % Y == 0` parses as `not ((X % Y) == 0)` which happens to be the intended meaning, but no disciplined reader should be asked to verify this at a glance. Write `nominal_dask_chunk_size % zw != 0` or parenthesize. The competent programmer is fully aware of the limited size of his own skull; do not spend it on operator precedence puzzles.

issues.description: Loop invariant is unstated and only the first chunk of each axis is checked; `dw[0]` is taken as representative of the whole tuple with no proof.
issues.detail: `dask_write_chunks[ax]` is a tuple of per-block sizes along that axis. The code inspects only `dw[0]` and decides the entire axis is safe or unsafe based on that one element. The invariant the author seems to assume is `all blocks in dw have the same size, except possibly the last`. That invariant must be stated, and the trailing block must be excluded explicitly. As written the check is `forall axes: dw[0] % zw == 0`, which is not the property the safety argument requires. TESTED-NOT-PROVED.

issues.description: Region branch silently skips the alignment check, even though region writes are exactly where misalignment causes data loss.
issues.detail: The per-axis alignment audit runs before the `if region is None` split, but only against `dask_write_chunks` derived from `z.shape`. In the region branch the rechunk is computed from `new_blockdim(s, c, r)` and assigned to `chunks`, which may differ from `dask_write_chunks`. So the very property the warning is supposed to guarantee — that the chunks actually written to the store are shard-aligned — is checked against a different chunking than the one that will be written. State the postcondition (writes are shard-aligned) and verify it on the chunking that will be written, not on a sibling computation.

issues.description: PR description openly asks the reviewer what the policy should be when config and shard size conflict; the code ships one policy (raise) without that question resolved.
issues.detail: The author writes: "What should we do when there's competition between the global config and shard shape of the zarr array? Would an exception be appropriate here, prompting the user to change the config?" This is the precondition/postcondition question, asked aloud, and answered with code before the answer is agreed. REFUSED until the policy is stated: either (a) shard shape wins silently with a warning, (b) config wins with a warning, or (c) conflict is a hard ValueError. Choose, document, then implement.

issues.description: Test `test_zarr_risky_shards_warns` asserts a `pytest.raises` but is named `_warns`; vocabulary drift between warning and exception again.
issues.detail: If the contract is that the user gets a Warning, the test should use `pytest.warns`. If the contract is that the user gets an exception, rename the test to `_raises`. The name and the assertion disagree, mirroring the underlying confusion in `core.py`.

issues.description: `max(1, z.dtype.itemsize)` guards against an itemsize of zero, a case that does not exist for any real numpy dtype.
issues.detail: Defensive guard with no stated precondition it is protecting. If a zero-itemsize dtype were possible the safe_chunk_size formula would still be wrong (it would silently claim 1 byte is enough). DEFENSIVE-AS-SUBSTITUTE for thinking about the dtype precondition. Remove or justify.

review.summary: The patch is UNREASONED in the structured-programming sense: the author has not stated the precondition under which the new alignment check should warn versus refuse, and the code reflects that uncertainty — a class named `PerformanceWarning` is `raise`d as an exception, followed by an unreachable `break`, and the PR description explicitly asks the reviewer what the policy should be. The dimensional analysis of `safe_chunk_size = np.prod(zarr_write_chunks) * itemsize` is incoherent for a per-axis check, the loop invariant treats `dw[0]` as representative of the whole tuple without justification, and the region branch escapes the audit entirely. None of this is unfixable; all of it is what happens when one writes the code before stating the spec. Decide the policy (warn-and-continue, or refuse-and-raise), pick the matching primitive, fix the formula, audit the region branch against the chunks actually written, and the patch becomes defensible.
